title: Why partials
text:
It is Friday afternoon. The designer drops by with good news: the video card on your site is getting a small refresh. A rounded thumbnail, a view count with thousands separators, the author’s name as a link. Fifteen minutes of work, they say. You open the templates folder and start counting. The home page has a card. The listing page has a card. The search results have a card. The “related videos” sidebar has a smaller card that is really the same card with a class on it. The email digest has a card too, and that one was copied from the listing page sometime last spring and never updated. You stop counting at fourteen.
Every one of those cards started as a copy and paste, because Jinja templates made copying easy and reuse awkward. In Python you would never tolerate fourteen copies of a function. You would write it once, give it parameters, and call it. jinja_partials lets templates do exactly that:
{% for v in videos %}
    {{ render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=v) }}
{% endfor %}
render_partial takes the path of a fragment file and the data it needs, renders it, and hands back safe HTML. The fragment sees video and nothing else. It cannot quietly depend on some page-level variable, because it never receives any. You can read its inputs at the call site, rename at the boundary (the loop’s v becomes the card’s video), and nest fragments inside fragments as deep as the design needs. The designer’s fifteen minutes become fifteen minutes.

But Jinja already has include and macro
It does, and both are nearly right, which is exactly why they are frustrating.
{% include %} is a copy and paste that happens at render time. The fragment receives the entire context of whoever included it: every variable on the page, whether the fragment needs it or not. Nothing at the call site tells you what the fragment reads. Rename a variable on one page and the fragment breaks on that page only, and the fix is a {% with %} wrapper around the include, which is a parameter list wearing a disguise.
{% macro %} gets the parameters right. The trouble is where macros live. A macro is defined inside a template file, so every page that wants the card has to {% import %} that file first. And a macro is not itself a template you can render. When HTMX asks your server for just one card to swap into the page, you cannot hand it a macro. With partials, the same video_square.html renders inside a page and also serves as a fragment response straight from a route, because it was a plain template all along.
The original back-and-forth on this question is preserved in issue #1, if you enjoy that sort of thing.


What is in the box

One registration call per app, at startup. Flask, Quart, FastAPI, Starlette, or any Jinja2 environment you have lying around.
A render_partial(template_name, **data) global inside every template. It returns Markup, so autoescaping leaves your fragment alone.
The same function callable from Python, which makes a partial the easiest thing in your app to unit test.
Async apps are welcome. Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette with enable_async=True environments render partials on a small thread pool tied to the app’s lifespan, and your templates do not change at all. The mechanics are in How it works, and they are more interesting than they sound.

Two minutes to install, then the Quickstart builds that video card properly, once.

title: Testing partials
text:
The designer’s refresh from Why partials has landed. The view count has thousands separators, the author is a link, and because there is one card instead of fourteen, the change was one file. The remaining question is how you know it is right on every page, and the pleasant answer is that you do not have to look at every page. A partial has an explicit list of inputs and produces a string, which is about the most testable shape a piece of a web app can have. No browser, no full page, no database; you need the fragment’s name and a few keyword arguments. The patterns below are the ones the library’s own suite uses, so they are known to work.

Flask
render_partial with no renderer falls back to flask.render_template, which needs an app and a request context. A fixture provides both, and every test after that is two lines:
import flask
import pytest
import jinja_partials


@pytest.fixture
def app():
    app = flask.Flask(__name__, template_folder='templates')
    jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)
    with app.test_request_context('/'):
        yield app


def test_video_square(app):
    html = jinja_partials.render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=FakeVideo())
    assert '12,500 views' in html
That assertion is the thousands separators from the refresh, checked once, on behalf of every page that renders the card. A bad template name raises jinja2.TemplateNotFound, so pytest.raises(TemplateNotFound) is the right assertion when you want to prove a rename did not leave a dangling reference behind.


FastAPI and Starlette
After registration, the bound function is the render_partial global on the environment. You can call it directly, and you do not need the app running:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

templates = Jinja2Templates(directory='templates')
app = FastAPI()
jinja_partials.register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)


def test_card_partial():
    render = templates.env.globals['render_partial']
    html = render('shared/partials/card.html', item={'title': 'Python Basics'})
    assert 'Python Basics' in html
Outside a lifespan, async environments render through a per-registration fallback pool, so a plain synchronous test function is enough. When you do want the full request path, with TestClient(app) as client: runs the lifespan; the pool is created on entry and shut down on exit, and the app can be started and stopped as many times as the suite likes. That re-entrancy is tested, because it was once broken.


Quart
Quart’s app.test_app() context runs the before_serving and after_serving hooks, which is where the render pool lives. Drive it with asyncio.run from an ordinary synchronous test:
import asyncio
from quart import Quart
import jinja_partials


def test_quart_partial():
    app = Quart(__name__, template_folder='templates')
    jinja_partials.register_quart_extensions(app)

    async def cycle():
        async with app.test_app():
            return app.jinja_env.globals['render_partial']('shared/partials/badge.html', tag='beginner')

    assert 'beginner' in asyncio.run(cycle())


Plain Jinja2
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader
import jinja_partials

env = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader('templates'), autoescape=True)
jinja_partials.register_environment(env, markup=True)


def test_fragment():
    html = env.get_template('home/index.html').render(videos=[FakeVideo()])
    assert '<img src=' in html
If a test is specifically about escaping, assert isinstance(result, Markup). render_partial returns markupsafe.Markup whenever markup=True, and a plain str when it is not, which is the difference between a rendered card and a page full of angle brackets.
One file, one test, fourteen pages covered. A partial that passes in isolation renders the same way everywhere, because it never borrows anything from the page that calls it, and How it works shows how little machinery that guarantee rests on.

title: Installation
text:
The whole library is one module with one dependency, so this page is short. Install it with uv or pip:
uv add jinja-partials
# or
pip install jinja-partials
One small trap right at the door: the PyPI name has a hyphen and the import has an underscore. Python packaging has its traditions.
import jinja_partials
The only runtime dependency is jinja2. The package is pure Python, fully typed, and ships a py.typed marker, so your editor and type checker know what render_partial returns before you do.

Python versions
Python 3.10 or newer. If you install on an older interpreter, pip does not refuse; it quietly hands you 0.3.0, the last release that supported 3.8 and 3.9. That version has Flask, plain Jinja2, and synchronous Starlette registration, but none of the Quart and FastAPI support or the lifecycle-managed Starlette registration this guide describes. If a function on these pages is mysteriously missing, check which version you actually got.


Bring your own framework
jinja_partials does not install Flask, Quart, FastAPI, or Starlette. It looks for each one at import time, uses it if present, and otherwise carries on without it. Install the framework you use alongside the library, in the same environment. If you call a registration function for a framework that is not there, you get a PartialsException that says so plainly, for example Install Quart to use register_quart_extensions. No mystery tracebacks from three layers down.


Check the install
python -c "import jinja_partials; print(jinja_partials.__version__)"
The version is read from the installed package metadata, so it always tells the truth about what is in the environment. With that done, the Quickstart is next.

title: Frameworks
text:
Your templates never find out which framework is running them. { render_partial(...) } looks identical in a Flask app from 2019 and a FastAPI app you started this morning. What changes is one registration line, and for the async frameworks, how you render the page that contains the partials. Register exactly once per app, at startup, and the rest of this page is about which line to write.

Flask
import flask
import jinja_partials

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)
Flask is the original home of this library, and it gets the richest behavior. This is the only path that renders partials through flask.render_template, so everything you expect in a page is also there in a partial: context processors, the template_rendered signal, g, request, and session. If a partial wants the current user from a context processor, this is the registration that gives it one.


Quart
from quart import Quart
import jinja_partials

app = Quart(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_quart_extensions(app)
Quart templates are async, which is where things get interesting (see the page-level rule below and How it works for the full story). Registration adds before_serving and after_serving hooks that create and later shut down a dedicated thread pool for rendering partials. Pages render with await render_template(...) exactly as they always did.


FastAPI
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

app = FastAPI()
templates = Jinja2Templates(directory='templates')
jinja_partials.register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)
Registration wraps the app’s lifespan, so the render pool exists for exactly as long as the app is serving and not a moment longer. If you already pass lifespan= to FastAPI, it keeps running, startup and shutdown both, and whatever state it yields still reaches your routes.


Starlette
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

templates = Jinja2Templates(directory='templates')
app = Starlette(routes=[...])
jinja_partials.register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app)
Read that last line twice. templates comes first, and app is a keyword. It is the reverse of the FastAPI call, for the historical reason that Starlette support predates the app-aware version and the signature kept its original first argument. Passing the app is optional but recommended: with it you get a pool tied to the lifespan and a working max_workers; without it, async renders go through a shared module-level pool and max_workers is ignored.


The page-level rule for async environments
Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette apps usually create their Jinja environment with enable_async=True. jinja_partials handles partials in those environments without any template changes. The page that contains them is your job, and there is exactly one rule: render it with await template.render_async(...) and return an HTMLResponse.
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse


@app.get('/')
async def index() -> HTMLResponse:
    template = templates.get_template('home/index.html')
    return HTMLResponse(await template.render_async(items=items))
The tempting alternative, templates.TemplateResponse(...), calls the synchronous render(). On an async template that means asyncio.run() being invoked from inside the event loop that is already running your request, and Python declines with RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop. The partials were never the problem; the page was. On a synchronous environment, TemplateResponse is perfectly fine and partials work the same way.
The FastAPI, Starlette, and Quart examples in the repository all follow this rule, so you can copy a working route rather than remembering it.


Plain Jinja2
No framework? A framework the library has not heard of? Rendering email templates from a worker process? Register with the environment directly:
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader
import jinja_partials

env = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader('templates'), autoescape=True)
jinja_partials.register_environment(env, markup=True)
The markup=True is not decoration. register_environment is the one registration function whose markup defaults to False, kept that way for backwards compatibility. With autoescaping on, the default inserts your fragment as escaped text, and you get a page full of visible angle brackets. Pass markup=True and move on with your life.


The declarative extension
PartialsJinjaExtension performs the same registration (always with markup=True) from the environment’s extensions list. It suits frameworks and settings files that configure Jinja declaratively rather than in code:
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader

env = Environment(
    loader=FileSystemLoader('templates'),
    extensions=['jinja_partials.PartialsJinjaExtension'],
)
On a Flask app you can add it with app.jinja_env.add_extension('jinja_partials.PartialsJinjaExtension'), and it works, with one subtlety. Partials then render through the Jinja environment rather than flask.render_template, so context processor values and the template_rendered signal are not applied inside them. g, request, and session are still there, because Flask installs those as environment globals rather than through context processors. If your partials read context processor values, use register_extensions(app) and keep the extension for environments that are not Flask.


The same table, at a glance









Registration
Partials render through
markup
Flask context processors in partials




register_extensions(app)
flask.render_template
always True
yes


register_quart_extensions(app)
app’s Jinja environment, lifespan-managed pool
always True
n/a


register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)
templates.env, lifespan-managed pool
always True
n/a


register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app)
templates.env, lifespan-managed pool
always True
n/a


register_starlette_extensions(templates)
templates.env, shared module pool
always True
n/a


register_environment(env, markup=...)

defaults to False

PartialsJinjaExtension
the environment it is loaded into
always True
no



Every row is built on the same primitive, generate_render_partial(renderer), and How it works shows how little code sits behind this table. When one of these paths misbehaves, Troubleshooting names the symptom and the fix.

Or browse the SKILL.md file.
      
    
  


SKILL.md
---
name: jinja-partials
description: Reusable HTML fragments for Jinja2 templates in Flask, Quart, FastAPI, Starlette, or any Jinja2 environment, through a render_partial() template global that renders a fragment file with explicitly passed data and nests freely. Use when adding jinja_partials or jinja-partials to an app, writing or refactoring templates that repeat markup, serving HTMX fragments, choosing between include, macro, and render_partial, or when a partial renders as escaped text, raises PartialsException or TemplateNotFound, or a FastAPI or Starlette route fails with "asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop".
license: MIT
compatibility: Python 3.10 or newer; depends only on jinja2. Flask, Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette are optional and must be installed separately.
---

# jinja-partials

Repeated HTML fragments in Jinja2 templates are hard to keep consistent. jinja_partials adds a `render_partial(template_name, **data)` global that renders a fragment file with exactly the keyword arguments you pass, returns `markupsafe.Markup` so autoescaping leaves it alone, and nests. Misconfiguration raises `jinja_partials.PartialsException`; a bad template name raises `jinja2.TemplateNotFound`.

# Install

`uv add jinja-partials` or `pip install jinja-partials`. Import as `jinja_partials`. Install your web framework yourself; the library never pulls one in.

# Use

```python
import flask
import jinja_partials

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)  # once, at startup, before serving
```

```html
{# templates/home/index.html #}
{% for v in videos %}
    {{ render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=v) }}  {# outer v becomes inner video #}
{% endfor %}
```

Other frameworks swap only the registration line (see the table). In a test, render a fragment directly: `templates.env.globals['render_partial']('shared/partials/card.html', item=item)`, or `jinja_partials.render_partial(name, **data)` inside a Flask request context.

# Rules

- A partial sees only the keyword arguments you pass it plus environment globals. It never inherits the caller's context the way `{% include %}` does; pass everything, and use `| default(...)` for optional inputs.
- Template names are paths relative to the templates root with forward slashes and the extension, as for `render_template`.
- `register_environment(env)` defaults to `markup=False`. With autoescaping on, that inserts the fragment as escaped text. Pass `markup=True`. Every other registration path and `PartialsJinjaExtension` already use `markup=True`.
- `register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app)` takes templates first and app as a keyword. The FastAPI order is `register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)`. Swapping them fails with `AttributeError: 'Starlette' object has no attribute 'env'`.
- Register once per app where it is built. A second `register_fastapi_extensions` or `register_starlette_extensions` call wraps the lifespan again, and a second Quart registration adds another pair of serving hooks. There is no idempotency guard.
- Only `register_extensions(app)` on Flask renders partials through `flask.render_template`, so only there do context processors and the `template_rendered` signal apply inside partials. `PartialsJinjaExtension` on a Flask app skips them, though `g`, `request`, and `session` remain available as environment globals.
- In FastAPI and Starlette with an `enable_async=True` environment, render the page with `await template.render_async(...)` and return `HTMLResponse`. `templates.TemplateResponse(...)` calls `asyncio.run()` inside the running loop and raises `RuntimeError`. Partials inside the page need no change.
- Partials in async apps render on a thread pool (`max_workers=4` default) and the caller blocks for the result. Nested partials render on their own thread and do not count against `max_workers`. Renders beyond the pool size queue; they do not fail.
- `render_partial` with no renderer falls back to `flask.render_template` and raises `PartialsException('No renderer specified')` when Flask is absent. Outside Flask, bind a renderer with `generate_render_partial`.
- Framework imports are optional; `register_*` raises `PartialsException('Install <Framework> to use ...')` when the framework is missing.

# Decision table

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Flask app | `jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)` |
| Quart app | `jinja_partials.register_quart_extensions(app, max_workers=4)` |
| FastAPI app | `jinja_partials.register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates, max_workers=4)` |
| Starlette app with lifespan-managed pool | `jinja_partials.register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app, max_workers=4)` |
| Starlette templates, no app | `jinja_partials.register_starlette_extensions(templates)` (shared module pool) |
| Plain Jinja2 or unsupported framework | `jinja_partials.register_environment(env, markup=True)` |
| Declarative environment config | `Environment(extensions=['jinja_partials.PartialsJinjaExtension'])` |
| Custom render pipeline | `env.globals.update(render_partial=jinja_partials.generate_render_partial(renderer))` |
| Fragment response for HTMX | return the partial from the route with the framework's normal render call |
| Flask context processors inside partials | `register_extensions(app)`, not the extension |

# API

- `render_partial(template_name, renderer=None, markup=True, **data) -> Markup | str`: the primitive. Raises `PartialsException` without a renderer when Flask is absent; raises `TemplateNotFound` for a bad name.
- `generate_render_partial(renderer, markup=True) -> Callable`: binds `renderer(template_name, **data) -> str`; install the result as the `render_partial` global.
- `register_extensions(app: Flask) -> None`: Flask; raises `PartialsException` if Flask is missing.
- `register_quart_extensions(app: Quart, max_workers=4) -> None`: Quart; pool created in `before_serving`, shut down in `after_serving`, stored in `app.extensions['jinja_partials_executor']`.
- `register_fastapi_extensions(app: FastAPI, templates: Jinja2Templates, max_workers=4) -> None`: wraps the lifespan; pool on `app.state.jinja_partials_executor`; an existing `lifespan=` keeps running.
- `register_starlette_extensions(templates: Jinja2Templates, app: Starlette | None = None, max_workers=4) -> None`: templates first; `max_workers` applies only with `app`.
- `register_environment(env: Environment, markup=False) -> None`: plain Jinja2, sync or async; pass `markup=True`.
- `PartialsJinjaExtension(environment)`: Jinja2 extension; calls `register_environment(environment, markup=True)`.
- `PartialsException(Exception)`: misconfiguration or missing framework.

# Output

Page template plus partial, and the rendered result:

```html
{# home/index.html #}            {# shared/partials/card.html #}
{% for item in items %}          <div class="card"><h3>{{ item.title }}</h3></div>
  {{ render_partial('shared/partials/card.html', item=item) }}
{% endfor %}
```

```html
<div class="card"><h3>Python Basics</h3></div>   <!-- correct: Markup inserted verbatim -->
<div class="card"><h3>Python Basics</h3></div>   <!-- escaped text: markup=False on register_environment -->
```

Fix order when something is wrong: confirm the registration call ran once at startup, then the template path, then that every variable the fragment reads was passed, then `markup=True` on the plain Jinja2 path, then the page-level `render_async` rule in async apps.

# Resources

- Documentation: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/>
- Frameworks: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/user-guide/frameworks.html>
- Troubleshooting: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/user-guide/troubleshooting.html>
- How it works: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/user-guide/how-it-works.html>
- API reference: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/reference/>
- llms.txt: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/llms.txt>
- llms-full.txt: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials/llms-full.txt>
- Source: <https://github.com/mikeckennedy/jinja_partials>

title: register_starlette_extensions()
text:
Register jinja_partials with Starlette templates.


Usage
Source


register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=None, max_workers=4)


If an app is provided, creates a dedicated ThreadPoolExecutor when the app’s lifespan starts and shuts it down when the lifespan exits - even if startup or shutdown raises - so the app can be started and stopped repeatedly; outside lifespan cycles, async renders use a per-registration fallback executor with the same max_workers. Without an app, partials render directly for sync environments, or via a shared module-level executor for async (enable_async=True) environments.


Parameters


templates: Jinja2Templates

The Jinja2Templates instance used for rendering.

app: Optional[Starlette] = None

Optional Starlette application instance for lifecycle management.

max_workers: int = 4

Maximum number of worker threads for rendering partials. Only used when app is provided. Defaults to 4.





Raises


 PartialsException

If Starlette is not installed.





Example
With lifecycle management (note that templates comes first):
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

templates = Jinja2Templates(directory='templates')
app = Starlette(routes=[...])
jinja_partials.register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app)
Without lifecycle management (backwards compatible):
jinja_partials.register_starlette_extensions(templates)

title: register_fastapi_extensions()
text:
Register jinja_partials with a FastAPI application.


Usage
Source


register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates, max_workers=4)


This creates a dedicated ThreadPoolExecutor for rendering partials in async environments. The executor is created when the app’s lifespan starts and is shut down when the lifespan exits - even if startup or shutdown raises - so the app can be started and stopped repeatedly (e.g. multiple TestClient cycles). Outside a lifespan cycle, partials render directly for sync environments, or via a per-registration fallback executor with the same max_workers for async (enable_async=True) environments.


Parameters


app: FastAPI

The FastAPI application instance.

templates: FastAPIJinja2Templates

The Jinja2Templates instance used for rendering.

max_workers: int = 4

Maximum number of worker threads for rendering partials. Defaults to 4.





Raises


 PartialsException

If FastAPI is not installed.





Example
Register during app setup:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

app = FastAPI()
templates = Jinja2Templates(directory='templates')
jinja_partials.register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)

title: register_environment()
text:
Register jinja_partials with a plain Jinja2 environment.


Usage
Source


register_environment(env, markup=False)


Use this for standalone Jinja2 usage or frameworks without dedicated support. Handles both sync and async (enable_async=True) environments.


Parameters


env: Environment

The Jinja2 Environment to make render_partial available in.

markup: bool = False

When True, wrap rendered partials in markupsafe.Markup. Defaults to False, so with autoescaping on, pass markup=True or the fragment is inserted as escaped text.





Example
Register with a standalone environment:
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader
import jinja_partials

env = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader('templates'), autoescape=True)
jinja_partials.register_environment(env, markup=True)

title: generate_render_partial()
text:
Create a render_partial function bound to a specific renderer.


Usage
Source


generate_render_partial(renderer: Callable[..., Any], markup: Literal[True] = ...) -> Callable[..., Markup]
generate_render_partial(renderer: Callable[..., Any], markup: Literal[False]) -> Callable[..., str]
generate_render_partial(renderer: Callable[..., Any], markup: bool) -> Callable[..., Union[Markup, str]]


Parameters


renderer: Callable[…, Any]

Callable that renders a template name plus keyword arguments to a string.

markup: bool = True

When True (the default), results are wrapped in markupsafe.Markup.





Returns


 Callable[…, Union[Markup, str]]

A callable with the same signature as render_partial that uses the bound renderer.





Example
Install a custom renderer as the render_partial global:
def renderer(template_name: str, **data) -> str:
    return env.get_template(template_name).render(**data)

env.globals.update(render_partial=jinja_partials.generate_render_partial(renderer))

title: PartialsException
text:
Raised when jinja_partials is misconfigured or a required web framework is not installed.


Usage
Source


PartialsException()


Every register_* function raises it when its framework cannot be imported, and render_partial raises it when called with no renderer outside Flask. A template that cannot be found raises jinja2.TemplateNotFound instead.


Example
Catch it to give a clearer startup error:
import jinja_partials

try:
    jinja_partials.register_quart_extensions(app)
except jinja_partials.PartialsException as e:
    raise SystemExit(f'jinja_partials setup failed: {e}')

[0.3.2] - 2026-06-11

Fixed

Async executor lifecycle is now exception-safe and re-entrant. Apps registered with register_fastapi_extensions, register_starlette_extensions, or register_quart_extensions can now start and stop repeatedly (e.g. multiple TestClient cycles) without failing, and an exception during a wrapped lifespan no longer leaks the executor (#14).
Renders that happen outside a lifespan/serving cycle now use a lazy per-registration fallback executor that honors max_workers, instead of degrading to a shared 4-worker pool.



Changed

The FastAPI and Starlette example apps now use enable_async=True environments and render pages via render_async, exercising the executor lifecycle.
Added more package keywords (Jinja, HTMX, components, fragments, and the supported frameworks) for better PyPI discoverability.

title: Jinja Partials
text:
Overview
Every Jinja2 app of a certain age has a fragment that got copied. A video card, a badge, a table row. It started life on one page, got pasted onto a second, then a third, and by the time the designer asks for a small refresh there are fourteen of them and two have quietly drifted. In Python this never happens, because you would write a function with parameters and call it from everywhere. jinja_partials gives your templates that same move:
{{ render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=v) }}
That one call renders the fragment file with the data you hand it, and nothing else, and gives back HTML that is safe to drop straight into the page. Fragments nest as deep as the design needs. Every input is visible at the call site. And because a partial is just a template, the same file can render inline inside a page and be served on its own to an HTMX swap.

title: Jinja Partials
text:
Documentation
The full documentation is available at mkennedy.codes/docs/jinja-partials. This README is the short version; the user guide tells the whole story:

Why partials - the fourteenth copy of a video card, and how render_partial differs from include and macro
Installation and the Quickstart, which builds that card properly, once
Frameworks - Flask, Quart, FastAPI, Starlette, plain Jinja2, the declarative extension, and the one rule async apps must follow
Troubleshooting - a field guide to every error and wrong output, with the fix for each
Testing partials, How it works, and the FAQ
API reference

Coding agents can load the agent skill or read llms-full.txt.

title: Jinja Partials
text:
Supported Frameworks
Your templates never find out which framework is running them. { render_partial(...) } looks the same in a Flask app from 2019 and a FastAPI app you started this morning. The only thing that changes is one registration line at startup:

Flask - register_extensions(app)
FastAPI - register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)
Starlette - register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app)
Quart - register_quart_extensions(app)
Any Jinja2 environment - register_environment(env)

Under every one of those is the same tiny primitive. The framework helpers only differ in how they find the Jinja environment and, for the async frameworks, how they keep a small render thread pool alive for exactly as long as the app is serving.

title: Jinja Partials
text:
Examples
The examples folder holds a runnable app for each framework:

Flask example - the complete video site from this README, with a layout, a listing page, and a small JSON database of videos
FastAPI example - an enable_async=True environment rendering cards with nested badge partials
Starlette example - the same cards and badges on Starlette, with lifespan-managed rendering
Quart example - the async Flask cousin, rendering the same cards through before_serving and after_serving hooks

The three async examples are deliberately small and nearly identical, so you can diff them and see that the templates are the part that does not change. The screenshot below is the Flask example, and every card on it is one partial file rendered in a loop:



Screenshot of the Flask example app showing a grid of video cards, each rendered from the same partial

title: Jinja Partials
text:
Installation
It’s just pip install jinja-partials (or uv add jinja-partials) and you’re all set with this pure Python package. The PyPI name has a hyphen and the import has an underscore, import jinja_partials, which is the first and only trap at the door.
Requires Python 3.10 or newer. On older interpreters pip does not refuse; it quietly hands you the 0.3.0 release, which predates the Quart and FastAPI support and the lifecycle-managed Starlette support described here. If a function on this page is mysteriously missing, check which version you actually got.

title: Jinja Partials
text:
Usage
Register jinja_partials with your framework once, where the app is built, before it starts serving. After that the render_partial function is simply there in every template, like url_for. The Frameworks page covers each option in more depth, including the page-level rule for async apps.

Flask
Flask is the original home of this library and gets the richest behavior. Partials render through flask.render_template, so context processors, g, request, and session all work inside them exactly as they do in a page.
import flask
import jinja_partials

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)


FastAPI
Registration wraps the app’s lifespan, so the render pool exists for exactly as long as the app is serving. If you already pass a lifespan= to FastAPI, it keeps running and whatever state it yields still reaches your routes.
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

app = FastAPI()
templates = Jinja2Templates(directory="templates")

jinja_partials.register_fastapi_extensions(app, templates)


Starlette
Read the last line twice: templates comes first and app is a keyword, the reverse of the FastAPI call. Starlette support predates the app-aware version and kept its original first argument. Passing the app is optional but recommended, because that is what ties the render pool to the lifespan.
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.templating import Jinja2Templates
import jinja_partials

templates = Jinja2Templates(directory="templates")
app = Starlette(routes=[...])

jinja_partials.register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app)


Quart
Quart templates are async, and registration adds before_serving and after_serving hooks that create and later shut down the pool that renders partials. Your pages keep using await render_template(...) as they always did.
from quart import Quart
import jinja_partials

app = Quart(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_quart_extensions(app)


One rule for async apps
Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette apps usually build their Jinja environment with enable_async=True. jinja_partials handles the partials inside those templates with no changes on your side. The page that contains them is your job, and there is exactly one rule: in FastAPI and Starlette, render it with await template.render_async(...) and return an HTMLResponse. The tempting templates.TemplateResponse(...) calls the synchronous render(), which tries to start an event loop inside the one already running your request, and Python declines with RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop. The partials were never the problem; the page was.
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse


@app.get('/')
async def index() -> HTMLResponse:
    template = templates.get_template('home/index.html')
    return HTMLResponse(await template.render_async(items=items))


Direct Jinja2 Environment
No framework, or one the library has not heard of? Register with the environment directly. The markup=True is not decoration: this is the one registration function whose markup defaults to False, and with autoescaping on, the default inserts your fragment as escaped text.
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader
import jinja_partials

environment = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader("templates"))
jinja_partials.register_environment(environment, markup=True)


Using the Jinja2 Extension (Declarative)
If your framework or settings file configures Jinja declaratively, PartialsJinjaExtension performs the same registration from the environment’s extensions list, always with markup enabled.

For Flask Applications
With Flask, add the extension to your app’s Jinja environment:
import flask
import jinja_partials

app = flask.Flask(__name__)

# Declarative registration with Flask
app.jinja_env.add_extension('jinja_partials.PartialsJinjaExtension')

# Alternative: traditional registration
# jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)

Note: With the extension approach, partials render directly through the Jinja environment rather than flask.render_template. That means Flask context processors (@app.context_processor) and the template_rendered signal do not apply inside partials (g, request, and session still work, since Flask installs them as environment globals). If your partials depend on context processors, use jinja_partials.register_extensions(app).



For Standalone Jinja2 Environments
For direct Jinja2 usage (without Flask):
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader

# Declarative registration - extension automatically registers render_partial
environment = Environment(
    loader=FileSystemLoader("tests/test_templates"),
    extensions=["jinja_partials.PartialsJinjaExtension"]
)
# render_partial is now available in templates, no additional setup needed!


When to Use the Extension Approach
Reach for the extension when the environment is configured somewhere you do not control the Python, such as a framework or settings file that takes a list of extension names, or when you are already stacking other Jinja2 extensions and want this one listed beside them. It always enables markup, so your partials come back as Markup objects and autoescaping leaves them alone.

section: Why not just use include or macro from Jinja?
text:
Why not just use include or macro from Jinja?
Because both are nearly right, which is exactly why they frustrate. {% include %} hands the fragment the entire page context, so nothing at the call site tells you what it reads. {% macro %} has proper parameters but must be imported into every page and is not a file you can render on its own, so it cannot answer an HTMX request by itself. Why partials tells the story, and the original debate is on issue #1.

title: PartialsJinjaExtension
text:
Jinja2 extension that automatically registers render_partial functionality.


Usage
Source


PartialsJinjaExtension(environment)


The extension automatically makes render_partial available as a global function in templates. By default, markup is enabled.


Note
Partials registered this way render directly through the Jinja2 environment rather than flask.render_template, so Flask context processors and the template_rendered signal do not apply inside partials (g, request, and session remain available because Flask installs them as environment globals). Flask apps that rely on context processors should use register_extensions instead.


Parameters


environment: Environment

The Jinja2 environment the extension is loaded into. Jinja2 passes this automatically when the class is listed in extensions=[…].





Example
Enable the extension on a Jinja2 environment:
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader

env = Environment(
    loader=FileSystemLoader('templates'),
    extensions=['jinja_partials.PartialsJinjaExtension'],
)
html = env.get_template('home/index.html').render(videos=videos)

title: API Reference
text:
Public API for jinja_partials: framework registration, partial rendering, and the Jinja2 extension.


Framework registration

Register render_partial with your web framework once at app startup.


register_extensions()

Register jinja_partials with a Flask application.

register_fastapi_extensions()

Register jinja_partials with a FastAPI application.

register_starlette_extensions()

Register jinja_partials with Starlette templates.

register_quart_extensions()

Register jinja_partials with a Quart application.

register_environment()

Register jinja_partials with a plain Jinja2 environment.




Rendering

Render partial templates directly or build framework-specific renderers.


render_partial()

Render a partial template and return the resulting HTML fragment.

generate_render_partial()

Create a render_partial function bound to a specific renderer.




Jinja2 extension

Declarative registration via the Jinja2 extension mechanism.


PartialsJinjaExtension

Jinja2 extension that automatically registers render_partial functionality.




Exceptions

Errors raised by jinja_partials.


PartialsException

Raised when jinja_partials is misconfigured or a required web framework is not installed.

title: register_extensions()
text:
Register jinja_partials with a Flask application.


Usage
Source


register_extensions(app)


Makes render_partial available as a global function in the app’s Jinja templates, rendering with flask.render_template.


Parameters


app: Flask

The Flask application instance.





Raises


 PartialsException

If Flask is not installed.





Example
Register once at startup:
import flask
import jinja_partials

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_extensions(app)

title: register_quart_extensions()
text:
Register jinja_partials with a Quart application.


Usage
Source


register_quart_extensions(app, max_workers=4)


This creates a dedicated ThreadPoolExecutor for rendering partials in async environments. The executor is created when the app starts serving and shut down when it stops, so the app can be started and stopped repeatedly (an executor left behind by a failed startup is replaced on the next start). Outside a serving cycle, partials render via a per-registration fallback executor with the same max_workers.


Parameters


app: Quart

The Quart application instance.

max_workers: int = 4

Maximum number of worker threads for rendering partials. Defaults to 4.





Raises


 PartialsException

If Quart is not installed.





Example
Register once at startup:
from quart import Quart
import jinja_partials

app = Quart(__name__)
jinja_partials.register_quart_extensions(app)

title: render_partial()
text:
Render a partial template and return the resulting HTML fragment.


Usage
Source


render_partial(template_name: str, renderer: Optional[Callable[..., Any]] = ..., markup: Literal[True] = ..., data: Any = {}) -> Markup
render_partial(template_name: str, renderer: Optional[Callable[..., Any]] = ..., markup: Literal[False], data: Any = {}) -> str
render_partial(template_name: str, renderer: Optional[Callable[..., Any]] = ..., markup: bool = ..., data: Any = {}) -> Union[Markup, str]


Parameters


template_name: str

Path of the template within the templates folder, e.g. shared/partials/video_image.html.

renderer: Optional[Callable[…, Any]] = None

Callable that renders the template with the given keyword arguments. Defaults to flask.render_template when Flask is installed.

markup: bool = True

When True (the default), wrap the result in markupsafe.Markup so it is not re-escaped when inserted into another template.

**data: Any

Model data passed to the template as keyword arguments.





Returns


 Union[Markup, str]

The rendered fragment as Markup, or str when markup=False.





Raises


 PartialsException

If no renderer is specified and Flask is not installed.





Example
Inside a template, after any register_* call:
{{ render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=v) }}
From Python in a Flask request context, for example in a test:
html = jinja_partials.render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=video)

title: FAQ
text:
Short answers, each with a link to the page that has the long one.

Why not just use include or macro?
Because each is nearly right in a different way. {% include %} hands the fragment the entire caller context, so nothing at the call site says what the fragment reads. {% macro %} has proper parameters but must be imported into every page and is not a file you can render on its own. Why partials tells the story, and issue #1 has the original debate.


Does this work with HTMX?
It is a natural pairing. A partial is an ordinary template, so a route can return it directly for an hx-get swap with flask.render_template('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=v), while your pages keep rendering the very same file inline with render_partial. One card, two delivery routes.


Can a partial extend a layout?
Yes. A partial is rendered like any other template, so {% extends %}, {% block %}, {% include %}, and macros all work inside it. The library’s test suite renders a partial that extends a layout, mostly to prove nobody accidentally forbids it.


Can I call render_partial from Python?
Yes, and it is the best way to test one. In a Flask request context, jinja_partials.render_partial(name, **data) goes through flask.render_template. For the other frameworks, the bound function is the render_partial global on the environment: templates.env.globals['render_partial'](name, **data). Testing partials shows both.


What does a partial see?
Only the keyword arguments you passed, plus the environment’s globals. On the Flask register_extensions path, context processors, g, request, and session are applied too, because partials render through flask.render_template there. Everywhere else, if you did not pass it, it is not there, by design.


Why is my fragment escaped?
render_partial returned a str instead of Markup. On the plain Jinja2 path, pass markup=True to register_environment. Troubleshooting has the details.


Do my templates change for async apps?
No. { render_partial(...) } is identical in Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette. The one change is at the page level in FastAPI and Starlette: render pages with await template.render_async(...) and return an HTMLResponse when the environment has enable_async=True. See the page-level rule.


Is the thread pool safe under load?
Yes. Each top-level partial render takes one worker while it runs and queues when the pool is full. Nested partials render on their own thread, so nesting depth cannot exhaust the pool. The pool is created when the app starts serving and shut down when it stops, including after a failed startup. How it works has the tiers and the reasoning.


What happens if I register twice?
On Flask and plain Jinja2, the second call simply replaces the global. On FastAPI and Starlette, each call wraps the lifespan again; on Quart, each call adds another pair of serving hooks. Register once, where the app is built.


Is there a version for other template languages?
For Pyramid and Chameleon, see chameleon_partials.


Which Python versions are supported?
3.10 and newer. Older interpreters get 0.3.0 from pip; see Installation.

title: How it works
text:
The whole library is one file, and you can read it in a coffee break. This page is the guided tour. There are three layers, and once you have seen them, every rule elsewhere in this guide stops being a rule to memorize and becomes an obvious consequence.

One primitive and some sugar
At the center is render_partial(template_name, renderer=None, markup=True, **data). It does two things. It calls renderer(template_name, **data), and if markup is true it wraps the result in markupsafe.Markup, which is Jinja’s way of saying “this string is already HTML, do not escape it again.” With no renderer it falls back to flask.render_template, and if Flask is not around either, it raises PartialsException rather than guess.
generate_render_partial(renderer, markup=True) is functools.partial over that function with the renderer baked in. Every register_* function in the library is the same three-step recipe: build a framework-specific renderer(template_name, **data) -> str, bind it, install the result as a Jinja global.
env.globals.update(render_partial=jinja_partials.generate_render_partial(renderer, markup=True))
That recipe is also the extension point. A framework the library has never heard of needs about three lines:
def renderer(template_name: str, **data) -> str:
    return my_env.get_template(template_name).render(**data)

my_env.globals.update(render_partial=jinja_partials.generate_render_partial(renderer))
Look at what the renderer receives: a name and data, nothing else. Each partial is rendered by its own renderer call with a fresh context built from data alone. That is the entire mechanism behind “a partial sees only what you pass it.” There is no context-hiding code anywhere, because there is no shared context to hide.


Markup defaults, and why one of them is different
render_partial and generate_render_partial default to markup=True. The framework registrations and PartialsJinjaExtension hardcode markup=True. register_environment alone defaults to markup=False, because it did when it was first released and changing it would silently alter output for existing users. So the plain Jinja2 path is the one place you have to say markup=True yourself. The type overloads encode all of this: markup=True returns Markup, markup=False returns str, and your type checker can tell you which you have.


Bridging async environments
Here is the interesting part. Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette apps typically build their Jinja environment with enable_async=True. A template in such an environment can only be rendered with await template.render_async(...). Meanwhile, { render_partial(...) } is a Jinja expression, evaluated synchronously in the middle of rendering the page, and a Jinja expression cannot await anything. So the partial needs an await, and the only place it can run from is a place that cannot await.
The way across is a thread. The renderer submits asyncio.run(template.render_async(**data)) to a ThreadPoolExecutor and blocks on the result. The worker thread has no event loop of its own, so asyncio.run is legal there and spins one up. The calling thread, which may well be the server’s event loop, waits for the fragment to come back. That wait is a deliberate tradeoff: partials are small and fast, and the alternative would be a different template syntax for async apps. Templates staying identical across frameworks is worth a short block.
Nesting adds a twist. A nested partial is rendered from inside a worker thread that is itself blocked, waiting for the outer render to finish. If the nested render were submitted to the same pool, it would be waiting for a worker while occupying one. Nest as deep as the pool is wide, or get enough concurrent requests doing it, and every worker is waiting for a worker, forever. That bug shipped in 0.3.2. Nested renders now run on a short-lived dedicated thread instead, so max_workers only bounds how many top-level partial renders are in flight at once, and nesting depth does not count against it.


Three executor tiers
Which pool a render lands in depends on how you registered and whether the app is serving.

A dedicated pool, created when the app starts serving and shut down when it stops. FastAPI and Starlette get it by wrapping app.router.lifespan_context; the pool is parked on app.state.jinja_partials_executor. Quart gets it through before_serving and after_serving hooks; the pool lives in app.extensions['jinja_partials_executor'].
A lazy per-registration fallback pool for renders outside a serving cycle, which mostly means tests that never start the app. It honors the same max_workers and is never shut down.
A module-level pool shared by register_environment, PartialsJinjaExtension, and register_starlette_extensions without an app. Four workers, never shut down.

The lifecycle is built to survive bad days. The dedicated pool is created inside the lifespan wrapper and shut down in a finally, so a startup that raises still cleans up and the app can start and stop repeatedly, which is what every TestClient context does. The app state is cleared before the pool shuts down, so a render racing with shutdown falls back to tier two instead of submitting to a dying pool. Quart’s startup hook replaces a stale pool left behind by a previous failed startup. Each of these has a test, and each test exists because the behavior was once missing.


Sizing max_workers
max_workers (default 4) on the Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette registrations sets the size of the dedicated and fallback pools. Each top-level partial render occupies one worker for the duration of that fragment. Renders beyond the pool size queue; they do not fail and they do not deadlock. Raise it if profiling shows requests waiting on partials under load, and leave it alone otherwise. It has no effect on register_starlette_extensions without an app or on the plain Jinja2 paths, which use the shared module-level pool.
That is the whole module. The FAQ answers the questions people usually have at this point.

title: Quickstart
Troubleshooting
text:
Think of this page as a field guide. Each entry starts with what you actually see, on the page or in a traceback, because that is what you have in front of you when you arrive here. Then the cause, then the fix. Most of them are one line.

The partial shows up as text, not HTML
What you see: the page displays <div> and friends literally, as if someone printed the template. View source shows <div>.
What happened: the environment has autoescaping on, render_partial returned a plain str instead of Markup, and Jinja did its job and escaped it. The guilty party is almost always the plain Jinja2 path, because register_environment defaults to markup=False. You can also get here by building your own renderer with generate_render_partial(renderer, markup=False).
The fix: pass markup=True to register_environment or generate_render_partial. The framework registrations and PartialsJinjaExtension already do. Resist the urge to sprinkle | safe over every call site; that fixes the symptom fourteen times and the cause zero times.


PartialsException: No renderer specified
What happened: render_partial was called from Python with no renderer argument, and Flask is not installed, so there was no default renderer to fall back to. This is the library telling you it does not know how to render anything yet.
The fix: inside a web app, register with your framework and use the global from templates. From Python, pass renderer= explicitly, or bind one once with generate_render_partial(renderer) as shown in custom renderers.


PartialsException: Install Flask to use register_extensions
There are Quart, FastAPI, and Starlette editions of this message too. You called a registration function, and its framework could not be imported in this interpreter. Often this is a second virtual environment, a Docker image missing a dependency, or a test runner with a different Python than the one you ran the app with.
The fix: install the framework into the same environment as jinja_partials. The library never installs frameworks on your behalf; see Installation.


AttributeError: ‘Starlette’ object has no attribute ‘env’
What happened: register_starlette_extensions was called with the app first, which is the FastAPI order. The function took your app, assumed it was a Jinja2Templates, and asked it for .env.
The fix: the Starlette signature is register_starlette_extensions(templates, app=app). Templates first, app as a keyword. Yes, it is the reverse of FastAPI; Frameworks explains why.


jinja2.exceptions.TemplateNotFound: shared/partials/video_square.html
What happened: the name you passed does not resolve against the environment’s loader. The error helpfully prints the name it looked for, so compare it character by character with the file on disk.
The fix: template names are paths relative to the templates root, forward slashes, extension included. Look for a stray leading slash, a missing subfolder, or a blueprint in Flask whose template_folder is not what you think it is.


jinja2.exceptions.UndefinedError: ‘video’ is undefined
What happened: the partial reads a variable the caller never passed. This is not a bug in the library; it is the library’s whole philosophy showing up in a traceback. Partials never see the caller’s context. {% include %} would have silently handed over the page’s video; render_partial makes you say it out loud.
The fix: pass every value the fragment needs as a keyword argument, render_partial('shared/partials/video_square.html', video=v). For optional inputs, let the fragment handle absence with | default(...), the way the thumbnail partial handles classes.


RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop
What happened: a FastAPI or Starlette route rendered the page with templates.TemplateResponse(...) or template.render(...) on an environment created with enable_async=True. Rendering an async template synchronously means calling asyncio.run() from inside the server’s event loop, which Python refuses. Note the word page: the partials inside it were not involved.
The fix: render the page with await template.render_async(...) and return an HTMLResponse. The partials need no change; jinja_partials renders them on its own thread pool. The page-level rule has the code.


Context processor values are missing inside a partial
What happened: on Flask, you registered with PartialsJinjaExtension, and partials render through the Jinja environment, which does not run @app.context_processor functions. g, request, and session still work on that path, which can make the missing value feel random. It is not; only context processors and the template_rendered signal are skipped.
The fix: use jinja_partials.register_extensions(app), the only registration that renders partials through flask.render_template.


A request hangs while rendering nested partials
What happened: in versions up to 0.3.2, a nested partial in an async app waited on the same thread pool its outer partial was sitting in. Nest as deep as max_workers, or get enough concurrent requests with nested partials at once, and every worker was waiting for a worker. The pool never recovered.
The fix: upgrade. Nested renders now run on their own short-lived thread, so nesting depth never counts against max_workers. If you cannot upgrade yet, raise max_workers well above the deepest nesting multiplied by the concurrency you expect.


The lifespan or startup hook runs twice
What happened: register_fastapi_extensions or register_starlette_extensions was called twice on one app. Each call wraps whatever lifespan is there, including the previous wrap; there is no idempotency guard. A second Quart registration likewise adds another pair of serving hooks. The usual culprit is an app factory that registers, plus a module that registers again at import.
The fix: register once, where the app is constructed, and make that the only caller.
